claims.claim: A church should be a community of people who live up to its standards, and those who do not should be put out.

stances.summary: The Church is Christ's pure bride. She must not even hear a promise of pardon for adultery; grave sinners after baptism belong outside her peace for good.
stances.quote: But it is in the church that this (edict) is read, and in the church that it is pronounced; and (the church) is a virgin! Far, far from Christ's betrothed be such a proclamation! She, the true, the modest, the saintly, shall be free from stain even of her ears.
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, 1885
stances.original: Sed hoc in ecclesia legitur, et in ecclesia pronuntiatur, et uirgo est. Absit, absit a sponsa Christi tale praeconium! Illa, quae uera est, quae pudica, quae sancta, carebit etiam aurium macula.
stances.context: Written in his Montanist years (c. 210-220), against a bishop's edict readmitting penitent adulterers (the bishop is unnamed; Callistus of Rome is only a scholarly guess). In the same chapter he says his side excommunicates the twice-married and dooms adulterers to "tears barren of peace". Chapter 21 draws the line between two churches: the Church "will forgive sins: but (it will be) the Church of the Spirit, by means of a spiritual man; not the Church which consists of a number of bishops." He did not change his mind about putting grave sinners out: as a Catholic (Apology 39, c. 197) he already describes "his severance from us in prayer, in the congregation and in all sacred intercourse". What changed is readmission: On Repentance 7-9 (Catholic period) allowed one public repentance after baptism; On Modesty withdraws it for adultery, murder and apostasy. Montanist, so outside the Catholic Church when he wrote this.

stances.summary: A true church knows whom it may take communion with. His own community put grave sinners out; Callistus's party took them in and gave communion to anyone.
stances.quote: whose school continues, preserving its customs and tradition, not discerning with whom they ought to communicate, but indiscriminately offering communion to all.
stances.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, 1886
stances.location: Book 9, chapter 7 in the ANF (9.12 in modern Greek editions)
stances.context: Written c. 222-235 against Callistus, bishop of Rome 217-222, whom Hippolytus opposed as a rival leader. In the same chapter he says sinners fled to Callistus after some of them, "in accordance with our condemnatory sentence, had been by us forcibly ejected from the Church", and he mocks Callistus's followers who "attempt to call themselves a Catholic Church!" He also objects that under Callistus a bishop guilty even of a sin unto death was not deposed. The whole chapter is polemic: Hippolytus is an enemy witness about Callistus, but his own stance is plain. Venerated as a martyr; the authorship of the Refutation is still debated by some scholars.

stances.summary: The Church is kept safe only by strict discipline, pushing back those who resist it. After 251 he would not give communion again to those who had sacrificed to idols.
stances.quote: so that it would appear that the Church's safety can be no otherwise secured, than by repelling any who set themselves against it as adverse waves, and by maintaining the ever-guarded rule of discipline itself as if it were the rudder of safety in the tempest.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, 1886
stances.work: Letter 30 in Cyprian's correspondence (the Roman clergy to Cyprian), written by Novatian
stances.context: Written in 250, before his schism, in the name of the Roman clergy; Cyprian says Novatian wrote it (Letter 51.5 in the ANF). The same letter still allows peace to the dying lapsed, so this is his moderate period. In 251 he broke with Cornelius and refused communion to the lapsed altogether (his circular letter, as reported by Socrates, Church History 4.28: do not admit them to the mysteries, leave their pardon to God). His followers took the name Cathari, "the pure": Eusebius, Church History 6.43.1, speaks of those who "call themselves Cathari". Condemned as a schismatic; Nicaea (canon 8) still had to legislate for his church in 325. His view on purity did not change; his view on readmission hardened.

stances.summary: God's law allows no breaking of a single commandment. Lambs must not share communion with wolves, and whoever consents to it is defiled.
stances.quote: according to the law of heaven it is not allowed to break one of the commandments, and that lambs ought not to hold communion with wolves, and that all consenting unto such is in fault, that he then who toucheth pitch is defiled
stances.translation: C. H. Collyns, The Extant Works of S. Pacian, Library of Fathers vol. 17, 1842
stances.work: His lost treatise, as quoted by Pacian of Barcelona, Letter 3 to Sympronian
stances.context: Sympronian was a Novatianist in Spain in the later 4th century. His treatise is lost; Pacian quotes these words in quotation marks in order to answer them, so they come to us through an opponent. In section 1 Pacian sums up the whole treatise: "that by the receiving of sinners she herself perishes." Not in the candidate pool; a schismatic.

stances.summary: Holiness belongs only to the righteous. The Church must keep the impious out, and sacraments from an unholy minister pollute rather than cleanse.
stances.quote: In the first Psalm David separates the blessed from the impious, not indeed making them into parties, but excluding all the impious from holiness.
stances.translation: J. R. King, revised by Chester D. Hartranft, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 1 vol. 4, 1887
stances.work: Letter to his clergy, as quoted by Augustine, Answer to the Letters of Petilian
stances.context: Petilian was the Donatist bishop of Cirta; his letter (c. 398-400) survives only because Augustine quotes it clause by clause in order to answer it. Same letter, Book 2 chapter 3 section 6: "For what we look to is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient." The Donatists held that bishops who had handed over the Scriptures in the persecution of 303-305 (traditores) had defiled everyone in communion with them, so the pure church was their own. Not in the candidate pool; a schismatic.

stances.summary: A sinner left in the Church infects the rest. A church that takes no action against sin shares the guilt, and not only for murder and adultery.
stances.quote: In Corinth the man that had his father’s wife, though accused of nothing else except this only, is not only himself handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh until he should correct his sin by worthy fruits of repentance, but involves the whole Church together in those accusations because it had taken no proceedings against the sin.
stances.translation: W. K. L. Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (London: SPCK, 1925)
stances.work: On the Judgment of God (De iudicio Dei), his preface to the Morals
stances.context: Addressed to Christians generally, not only monks. On the page before he says that, unless the sinning soul "be utterly cut off", its sin does not stay with it alone "but infects also those who have not manifested zeal for good" (the OCR prints "1t" for "it" there, so it is not given as the quote). He then blames the "perverted tradition" that rebukes murder and adultery but tolerates anger, slander, drunkenness and greed. His monastic Shorter Rules go further (no. 44: a monk who stays sullen when woken is to be "cut off from the body as a rotten and corrupt branch"). Yet he was no Novatianist: his canonical letters (188, 199, 217) set years of exclusion and then readmit, and Letter 217 canon 84 says the manner of repentance matters more than its length. The 1925 English is public domain in the US (published before 1929). Clarke's pages carry OCR noise; the quoted lines are clean.

stances.summary: Known, open sinners must be kept from the Lord's table, even an emperor. He would sooner die than give the Lord's blood to the unworthy.
stances.quote: I would give up my life rather than impart of the Lord's blood to the unworthy; and will shed my own blood rather than impart of such awful blood contrary to what is meet.
stances.translation: George Prevost, revised by M. B. Riddle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 1 vol. 10, 1888
stances.context: Preached at Antioch c. 390, to the clergy who distribute communion: "Though any one be a general, though a deputy, though it be he himself who is invested with the diadem, and come unworthily, forbid him". Two limits: he speaks only of "open sinners", leaving the hidden to God; and the aim is restoration: "not that we repel them only, nor cut them off, but in order that we may amend them, and bring them back". Elsewhere he calls the church "a place of healing, not a law court" (Homilies on Repentance 3; see the second-chances file), so he is strict about the table, not a purist about membership. His Homily 46 on the wheat and tares reads the tares as heretics and forbids killing them, which is a different question.

stances.summary: Only those who believe, are baptized and live as Christ commanded may share the Eucharist.
stances.quote: of which no one is allowed to partake but the man who believes that the things which we teach are true, and who has been washed with the washing that is for the remission of sins, and unto regeneration, and who is so living as Christ has enjoined.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 150-155 to the emperor, describing Christian practice. A plain rule for admission to the Eucharist, not an argument about expelling members; it shows the standard was holy living, not only right belief.

stances.summary: Christians test people before admitting them, appoint members to watch over conduct, and keep those who live shamefully out of the assembly.
stances.quote: among these there are certain persons appointed to make inquiries regarding the lives and behaviour of those who join them, in order that they may prevent those who commit acts of infamy from coming into their public assembly, while those of a different character they receive with their whole heart, in order that they may daily make them better.
stances.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 248, defending the Church against the pagan Celsus. The same chapter says the dissolute are excluded from the community and mourned "as dead", but received back after a change of life, though never again given office. So strict on discipline, open to return. I did not verify the often-cited line in his Homilies on Joshua (21.1) that the Church cannot be fully purified while on earth: no pre-1929 English was checked, so it is left out. Some of Origen's other teachings were condemned in 553.

stances.summary: After the time for repentance, God will purify His Church by casting out the wicked, the hypocrites and the waverers, and it will be one body of the pure.
stances.quote: In like manner also shall it be with the Church of God, after it has been purified, and has rejected the wicked, and the hypocrites, and the blasphemers, and the waverers, and those who commit wickedness of different kinds. After these have been cast away, the Church of God shall be one body, of one mind, of one understanding, of one faith, of one love.
stances.translation: F. Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Early 2nd century, Rome. A vision of the Church as a tower from which unfit stones are rejected. The purifying is God's act, after a set time; Hermas also teaches one repentance after baptism (Mandate 4.3), so the mood is urgency, not a rule for bishops to expel. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: A monk suspended for a fault is cut off from common prayer until he has done penance and been publicly forgiven; anyone who prays with him first shares his condemnation.
stances.quote: if one of them has been suspended from prayer for some fault which he has committed, no one has any liberty of praying with him before he performs his penance on the ground, and reconciliation and pardon for his offense has been publicly granted to him by the Abbot before all the brethren.
stances.translation: Edgar C. S. Gibson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Written c. 420, describing with approval the practice of the Egyptian monasteries. About a monastic community, not the whole Church, and the exclusion is temporary and ends in public reconciliation.

stances.summary: When every remedy has failed, the abbot must cut off the brother who will not amend, so that one sick sheep does not infect the flock.
stances.quote: then at last the abbot may use the pruning knife, as the apostle says: "Remove evil from you," etc.: lest one diseased sheep contaminate the whole flock.
stances.translation: Ernest F. Henderson, Select Historical Documents of the Middle Ages (London: George Bell, 1892)
stances.context: Written c. 530-540 for monks. Expulsion is the last step, after warnings, excommunication, blows and the prayer of the whole community; chapter 27 tells the abbot to send "secret consolers" to the excommunicated brother, and chapter 29 takes a departed brother back up to three times. A community with standards, run with mercy.

stances.summary: He refused communion with bishops who had pressed for a heretic's execution, grieved when he gave in for an hour to save lives, and avoided their company for the rest of his life.
stances.quote: he was filled with mourning and lamentation that he had even for an hour been mixed up with the evil communion
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Written c. 404 by Sulpicius, who knew Martin. The events are of 385-386: bishops led by Ithacius had pressed for the execution of Priscillian. Martin took communion with them once, only to save men already condemned, and "from that time forward, he carefully guarded against being mixed up in communion with the party of Ithacius"; he never attended a synod again. Words are the biographer's, not Martin's. It concerns bishops stained with blood, not ordinary sinners in the pews.

stances.summary: Baptism washes the Church clean of every spot and wrinkle, and the Lord wants her to stay that pure.
stances.quote: It has, says he, been asserted by me — but in such a sense that the Church is by the laver cleansed from every spot and wrinkle, and in this purity the Lord wishes her to continue.
stances.translation: Peter Holmes and Robert Ernest Wallis, revised by Benjamin B. Warfield, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 1 vol. 5, 1887
stances.work: His answer at the Synod of Diospolis (415), as quoted by Augustine, On the Proceedings of Pelagius
stances.context: The charge was that he taught "the Church here is without spot or wrinkle"; this is his reply as recorded in the synod's acts. Augustine at once links the charge to the Donatists and answers that the Church on earth must still pray "Forgive us our debts". Pelagius speaks of the ideal of a sinless Church, not of expelling members; count it as weak. Condemned as a heretic (Carthage 418; Ephesus 431).

stances.summary: No one may leave the Church because it has tares, or try to sort wheat from tares by human judgment; that belongs to Christ. But a flock must separate from a bishop who has sinned gravely.
stances.quote: nor may any one claim to himself what the Father has given to the Son alone, so as to think that he can take the fan for winnowing and purging the threshing-floor, or can separate by human judgment all the tares from the wheat. That is a proud obstinacy and a sacrilegious presumption which a depraved madness assumes to itself.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, 1886
stances.work: Letter 50, to the confessors Maximus and others (Letter 54 in modern numbering)
stances.context: Written 251 to Roman confessors returning from Novatian's schism. The same section opens: "For although there seem to be tares in the Church, yet neither our faith nor our charity ought to be hindered, so that because we see that there are tares in the Church we ourselves should withdraw from the Church". Letter 51.25 (to Antonianus) repeats the point against Novatian. The other side of Cyprian, c. 254-255, Letter 67.3, on two lapsed Spanish bishops: "a people obedient to the Lord's precepts, and fearing God, ought to separate themselves from a sinful prelate, and not to associate themselves with the sacrifices of a sacrilegious priest" (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/050667.htm). He also kept the lapsed out of communion until long penance was done. So: a mixed flock, a pure clergy. The Donatists later quoted this second Cyprian against the Catholics, and Augustine quoted the first.

stances.summary: Keep away from presbyters who live wickedly and follow those of blameless life; but those who split the Church for their own reasons do more harm than any reform they could bring.
stances.quote: For no reformation of so great importance can be effected by them, as will compensate for the mischief arising from their schism.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 180. The sentence ends a warning against those "who for trifling reasons, or any kind of reason which occurs to them, cut in pieces and divide the great and glorious body of Christ". The other side, Book 4, chapter 26, section 4, on presbyters who "serve their own lusts": "From all such persons, therefore, it behooves us to keep aloof" (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103426.htm). He is not writing about the moral purity of ordinary members either way.

stances.summary: A pastor should not deal with every fault the same way: some faults, even known ones, are wisely borne for a time, others hunted out and sharply rebuked.
stances.quote: It should be known too that the vices of subjects ought sometimes to be prudently connived at, but indicated in that they are connived at; that things, even though openly known, ought sometimes to be seasonably tolerated, but sometimes, though hidden, be closely investigated; that they ought sometimes to be gently reproved, but sometimes vehemently censured.
stances.translation: James Barmby, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 12, 1895
stances.context: Written c. 590 for bishops. It is about the timing of correction, not about expelling members, so it is weak evidence for this claim. The chapter goes on: "For sores by being unseasonably cut are the worse enflamed". I found no public-domain English of the Gregory line often cited on the good and the bad living together in the Church (Homilies on the Gospels), so it is not used.

stances.person: Callistus of Rome (as reported by his opponent Hippolytus)
stances.summary: Christ said to let the tares grow with the wheat. Noah's ark held clean and unclean animals together, and so does the Church; sinners should stay in it.
stances.quote: let those who in the Church are guilty of sin remain in it. But also he affirmed that the ark of Noe was made for a symbol of the Church, in which were both dogs, and wolves, and ravens, and all things clean and unclean; and so he alleges that the case should stand in like manner with the Church.
stances.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, 1886
stances.location: Book 9, chapter 7 in the ANF (9.12 in modern Greek editions)
stances.context: Callistus, bishop of Rome 217-222 and a martyr, left no writings. This is a hostile summary by his rival, written to condemn him; treat the wording as Hippolytus's. Hippolytus also says Callistus would not depose a bishop even for a sin unto death. Not in the candidate pool. It is the earliest known use of the wheat and tares and the ark for a mixed church, the two images later used by Cyprian, Jerome, Optatus and Augustine.

stances.summary: In this age the Church holds wheat and tares together, even among her bishops. The good must bear with the bad and the bad must change; the angels will sort them at the harvest.
stances.quote: I tell you of a truth, my Beloved, even in these high seats there is both wheat, and tares, and among the laity there is wheat, and tares. Let the good tolerate the bad; let the bad change themselves, and imitate the good.
stances.translation: R. G. MacMullen, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 1 vol. 6, 1888
stances.location: Sermon 23 in NPNF (Sermon 73 in the Benedictine numbering), section 4
stances.context: The same section: "We in this time present are like those servants of whom it was said, Will You that we go and gather them up? ... But it has been told us, Let both grow together until the harvest." His fullest statement, City of God 20.9 (c. 425): "Consequently, where both classes exist, it is the Church as it now is, but where only the one shall exist, it is the Church as it is destined to be when no wicked person shall be in her." (Latin, thelatinlibrary.com/augustine/civ20.shtml: "Ac per hoc ubi utrumque genus est, ecclesia est, qualis nunc est; ubi autem illud solum erit, ecclesia est, qualis tunc erit, quando malus in ea non erit.") City of God 1.35: false Christians are "thronging the churches with us, tomorrow crowding the theatres with the godless". He argued this for decades against the Donatists. He still backed excommunication for notorious sin. The twist: tolerant of sinners inside, he came to support the state forcing the Donatist separatists back; Letter 93.17 says "originally my opinion was, that no one should be coerced into the unity of Christ" (a change of mind about force, not about this claim).

stances.summary: Noah's ark is the Church: as it held leopards with kids and wolves with lambs, so the Church holds the righteous and sinners together.
stances.quote: As in the ark there were all kinds of animals, so also in the Church there are men of all races and characters. As in the one there was the leopard with the kids, the wolf with the lambs, so in the other there are found the righteous and sinners
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: An early work (c. 379), a dialogue in which Jerome speaks as "Orthodoxus". The dispute is over receiving back bishops and people who had been in communion with Arians; the Luciferians refused them. The sentence continues: "that is, vessels of gold and silver with those of wood and of earth." Jerome was severe about personal morals all his life (his letters are full of rebukes), but on who belongs in the Church he took the mixed view here.

stances.summary: Bishops may not do what the apostles were forbidden to do: sort the tares from the wheat. Christ ordered both to grow together until the harvest, and judgment is His.
stances.quote: For it would be a sin for us Bishops to do now, that which was not done by the Apostles, who were not permitted either to separate seeds or to pluck up the tares from the wheat.
stances.translation: O. R. Vassall-Phillips, The Work of St. Optatus against the Donatists (London: Longmans, 1917)
stances.context: Written against the Donatist bishop Parmenian (first edition c. 366-367; Book 7 was added in a later edition c. 384, and some scholars doubt parts of it). The chapter also says: "Let us recognise that we all are men; let no one usurp to himself the power of Judgement that belongs to God." The page prints the translator's footnote numbers and page markers inside the text; the quoted sentence has none. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: Those who call themselves the pure and shrink from penitent sinners are proud; no one is pure, and the whole Church, bad and good, is mixed in one lump to be made new.
stances.quote: You cannot, forsooth, endure the tears of the weepers; your eyes cannot bear the coarse clothing, the filth of the squalid; with proud eyes and puffed-up hearts you delicate ones say with angry tones, Touch me not, for I am pure.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 10, 1896
stances.context: Written c. 384-394 against the Novatianists. "Touch me not, for I am pure" is Ambrose putting words in their mouths (echoing Isaiah 65:5), not a quotation of them. Section 38: "Do you, Novatian, dare to call yourself pure". Book 1, 15.83: "we all, both bad and good, are mingled with the meal of the Church that we all may be a new lump." He still believed in real public discipline: he required public penance of the emperor Theodosius in 390.

stances.summary: Paul put out only the one sinner and left the church's peace whole. The Novatianists condemn every church for the sake of one sinner.
stances.quote: Mark, brother, first that he condemns not those with whom this man is in communion. He alone who had done this deed, is delivered to Satan, he only is excommunicated, the peace of the Saints being kept entire. Ye for one sinner condemn all churches.
stances.translation: C. H. Collyns, The Extant Works of S. Pacian, Library of Fathers vol. 17, 1842
stances.work: Letter 3 to Sympronian (Against the treatise of the Novatians)
stances.context: Written in the later 4th century by the bishop of Barcelona. He accepts that the unrepentant sinner is excommunicated (1 Corinthians 5), but not that a church which keeps sinners is defiled, and he notes that Paul later forgave the same man. Section 1 answers the Novatian claim "that by the receiving of sinners she herself perishes" with: "To reject the guilty; to flee the touch of sinners; to have so little confidence in her own innocence!" Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: Those who call themselves pure and refuse the penitent are new Pharisees, sick with the same failings as everyone else.
stances.quote: But what do you say, O new Pharisee pure in title but not in intention, who dischargest upon us the sentiments of Novatus, though you share the same infirmities? Will you not give any place to weeping? Will you shed no tear?
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 7, 1894
stances.context: Preached at Constantinople at Epiphany, probably 381, against the Novatianists ("pure in title" plays on their name, Cathari). He takes a deliberate middle line in the same section: "both are alike evil, indulgence not regulated by prudence, and condemnation that will never forgive". Section 19 adds that he too would refuse the unrepentant. So he rejects the pure church, not discipline.

stances.summary: Called to a meeting to judge a brother who had sinned, he came carrying a leaking basket of sand: his own sins trailing behind him. The monks let the brother go.
stances.quote: [The sands are] my sins "which are running down behind me and I cannot see them, "and I, even I, have come this day to judge shortcomings
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (London: Chatto and Windus, 1907), translated from the Syriac of Anan-Isho
stances.context: Scete, late 4th century. Budge prints a quotation mark at the start of every line of speech, so the quote has stray marks. Clean reading: "[The sands are] my sins which are running down behind me and I cannot see them, and I, even I, have come this day to judge shortcomings which are not mine." The saying ends: "they set free that brother and said nothing [further] to him." It is about refusing to judge a sinning brother in a community gathered to judge him; it is also used in the second-chances file.

stances.summary: When a priest drove a sinning brother out of church, Bessarion got up and walked out with him: if one sin makes a man unfit, he, with many, was less fit still.
stances.quote: On one occasion a brother committed sin in the church, and the priest drove him out therefrom, and there was there a man of discretion whose name was Bessarion, and he also arose and went out of the church, and said, " If ye have judged that " this man who hath committed only one offence is not fit to "worship God, how very much less fit am I
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (London: Chatto and Windus, 1907), translated from the Syriac of Anan-Isho
stances.context: Egypt, 4th-5th century; not in the candidate pool but the most exact desert answer to this claim. Budge's line-initial quotation marks appear inside the quote; clean reading of the speech: "If ye have judged that this man who hath committed only one offence is not fit to worship God, how very much less fit am I, who have committed many sins, to do so?" This scan of the same 1907 edition has cleaner OCR here than the one used for Moses and Antony.

stances.summary: When a monastery refused to take back a brother who had fallen and been expelled, Antony asked them whether they would drown a ship just saved from a storm; they took him back.
stances.quote: Do ye wish to drown him that hath been saved?
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (London: Chatto and Windus, 1907), translated from the Syriac of Anan-Isho
stances.context: Antony died in 356. The brother had fallen and been "expelled from that place"; after time with Antony he was sent back and the monks "cast him out" again. Antony's message: "A storm rose up against a ship on the sea, and destroyed the freight which she carried, but with the greatest difficulty she was saved [and brought] to land." It is about taking back the repentant rather than about the first expulsion, so strength 1; the same line is in the second-chances file.

stances.summary: The body of Christ has two parts in this age, like the bride who is "dark and comely": the bad part lives inside the Church, not outside it.
stances.quote: For far be it that the Church, which has no spot or wrinkle, which the Lord cleansed for Himself with His own blood, should be dark in any part, except in the left-hand part, through which the name of God is blasphemed among the nations. [...] But we cannot say that the tent of Kedar is outside the Church.
stances.translation: Own rendering from the Latin edited by F. C. Burkitt, The Book of Rules of Tyconius (Cambridge, 1894)
stances.original: absit enim ut Ecclesia quae non habet maculam aut rugam, quam Dominus suo sanguine sibi mundauit, aliqua ex parte fusca sit nisi in parte sinistra per quam nomen Dei blasphematur in gentibus. [...] non possumus autem dicere tabernaculum Cedar praeter Ecclesiam esse.
stances.location: Rule 2, "Of the twofold body of the Lord" (Burkitt p. 10)
stances.context: Written c. 380 by a Donatist layman who nonetheless taught a mixed Church. Augustine says he "has written most triumphantly against the Donatists" while remaining one (On Christian Doctrine 3.30.42); his clash with the Donatist bishop Parmenian is known from Augustine's Against the Letter of Parmenian, which was not checked here. Augustine took over this rule and renamed it: "the true and the mixed body of the Lord" (On Christian Doctrine 3.32.45). The only English is modern (Babcock 1989), so the rendering is mine. The Latin is cleaned from archive.org OCR: the page reads "mun- 15 dauit", "Der" for Dei and "Kcclesiam", with margin references ("Gants", "Rois") run into the text; "Cedar" is Kedar of Song of Songs 1:5. A Donatist, so a schismatic, though on this point he sided with the Catholics.

splits_fathers: Real voices on both sides, and it was one of the great fights of the early Church: three schisms turned on it (Hippolytus against Callistus in Rome c. 220; Novatian's "Cathari" from 251; the Donatists in Africa from 311 to Augustine's day). The pure-church side: Tertullian in his Montanist years, Hippolytus, Novatian and the Novatianists (Sympronian, Acesius), and the Donatists (Petilian, Parmenian). The mixed-church side, which became the settled view of the Great Church: Callistus (as his enemy reports him), Cyprian against Novatian, Optatus, Pacian, Ambrose, Gregory of Nazianzus, Jerome and above all Augustine, plus the Donatist Tyconius. Their proof texts were the wheat and tares, the dragnet, Noah's ark, and the great house with vessels of gold and of clay. But nearly everyone, on both sides, practised exclusion from communion for grave public sin. The mainstream difference was that exclusion was a medicine with a road back, and that the Church's holiness did not depend on getting rid of every sinner. Inside the mainstream there is a strict wing that sounds close to the claim: Basil's On the Judgment of God (a church that tolerates sin shares its guilt), Chrysostom barring open sinners from the table, Justin and Origen describing a Church that screened its members, and the monastic rules (Basil, Cassian, Benedict) that expel the incorrigible as a last resort. The desert tradition leans the other way in its stories: Moses the Black, Bessarion and Antony all refuse to see a fallen brother put out. On clergy the split runs differently: Cyprian (Letter 67), Martin of Tours and Irenaeus (4.26) wanted unworthy clergy removed or avoided, while Callistus reportedly would not depose a bishop even for mortal sin.
splits_people_today: As worded, most ordinary people today would disagree. The common expectation, inside and outside the churches, is that a church welcomes people as they are, and "judgmental" is one of the most frequent complaints about Christians. Those who would agree are a real but smaller group: churches that practise formal church discipline and membership covenants (many Reformed, Baptist and other evangelical congregations), Anabaptist communities with the ban and shunning (Amish, some Mennonites), Jehovah's Witnesses with disfellowshipping, and Catholics and Orthodox who favour withholding communion from public sinners (the recurring rows over communion for politicians or the remarried). Non-believers split in an interesting way: many dislike exclusion, yet the charge that churches are "full of hypocrites" is itself a purist complaint. The answer flips when the question is about leaders: after the abuse scandals most people, Christian or not, would say a pastor or priest who commits serious sin must be removed. So the claim is a useful divider only if it is about ordinary members, and it will lean one-sided (towards disagree) unless it is sharpened. I have no survey numbers for this; these are qualitative judgments.

misattributions.line: The church is a hospital for sinners, not a museum for saints.
misattributions.truth: Not found in any patristic work read for this file, and no patristic source is known. The second-chances research file records that secondary sources trace it to a 1964 newspaper advice column (Abigail Van Buren); that origin was not checked here either. The nearest genuine line is Chrysostom, Homilies on Repentance 3: the church is 'a place of healing, not a law court' (see the second-chances file).

misattributions.line: Touch me not, for I am pure.
misattributions.truth: Ambrose, On Repentance 1.8.37, putting words in their mouths (an echo of Isaiah 65:5). It is Ambrose's caricature, not a Novatianist text.

misattributions.line: How can he remit sins, who is himself a sinner? How can an impious man make a man holy?
misattributions.truth: In Jerome's Dialogue against the Luciferians (section 5) these words are spoken by the Luciferian, the side Jerome is refuting. Jerome's own view is the opposite (section 22, the ark).

misattributions.line: Let those who in the Church are guilty of sin remain in it (and the ark with dogs, wolves and ravens).
misattributions.attributed_to: Callistus of Rome, quoted as his own words
misattributions.truth: Callistus left no writings. The wording is his enemy Hippolytus's summary (Refutation 9.7 ANF, 9.12 Greek), written to condemn him. Cite it as Hippolytus reporting Callistus.

misattributions.line: I remit, to such as have discharged (the requirements of) repentance, the sins both of adultery and of fornication.
misattributions.truth: Quoted by Tertullian, On Modesty 1, from an unnamed bishop he mockingly calls 'the Pontifex Maximus'. The identification with Callistus is a scholarly guess; some scholars propose a bishop of Carthage instead.

misattributions.line: corpus permixtum (the Church as a 'mixed body')
misattributions.truth: A modern shorthand. In the English checked here Augustine speaks of 'the true and the mixed body of the Lord' and suggests the heading 'Concerning the mixed Church' (On Christian Doctrine 3.32.45), renaming the Donatist Tyconius's rule 'Of the twofold body of the Lord' (De Domini corpore bipertito, checked in Burkitt's Latin). Quote the sentence, not the two-word slogan. The Latin of Augustine's sentence was not checked.

misattributions.line: The Church is a whore, but she is my mother.
misattributions.truth: Not found in any Augustine text read for this file, and I could not search further. Treat it as unsourced and do not use it. (It may descend from the patristic image of the Church as Rahab, the 'chaste harlot', but that was not verified here.)

notes:
LEADS CHECKED. Tertullian, On Modesty: holds (chapters 1, 18, 21), Montanist. Hippolytus against Callistus: Refutation 9.7 in the ANF (9.12 in Greek editions); the tares and the ark are there, as Hippolytus's report. Cyprian's tares line is Letter 50 in the ANF (54 in modern numbering), section 3, not 51; Letter 51 (to Antonianus) section 25 makes the same point against Novatian. Letter 67 is the counterweight (separate from a sinful bishop). Novatian's own words survive only in Letter 30 of Cyprian's correspondence; the name Cathari is in Eusebius 6.43.1. Augustine: City of God 18.49 (the dragnet), 20.9 (the Church as it now is and as it will be), 1.35 (thronging the churches today, the theatres tomorrow), Letter 93 (tares; change of mind on force at 93.17) and Sermon 23 NPNF (73 Benedictine) all hold. Answer to Petilian is in NPNF; Against the Letter of Parmenian has no public-domain English and was not used. Optatus holds (Book 7.2, Vassall-Phillips 1917 on tertullian.org). Jerome, Dialogue against the Luciferians 22 holds.

BEYOND THE LEADS. Basil's On the Judgment of God (Clarke 1925, public domain in the US) is the strongest mainstream voice for the claim and is little known. Pacian's letters to the Novatianist Sympronian give both sides in one place. Tyconius (a Donatist who taught the mixed Church) and Bessarion (walked out of church with an expelled sinner) are the most striking voices on the no side outside the pool. Martin of Tours refusing communion with the bishops behind Priscillian's execution is a strong yes, but about bishops.

HOW TO READ THE SIDES. Almost every Father practised exclusion for grave public sin, so "agree" here means someone argued for purity of the membership or for putting people out as a principle, and "disagree" means someone argued the Church on earth is necessarily mixed and must not purge itself. Several on the disagree side (Augustine, Ambrose, Pacian, Gregory of Nazianzus) still upheld temporary excommunication; several on the agree side (Chrysostom, Origen, Benedict, Cassian, Basil) also received the repentant back. The context fields say which.

SUGGESTIONS FOR THE QUIZ WRITER. (1) The claim as worded will split the Fathers well (purists against the mixed-church majority) but ordinary people today mostly one way. A sharper everyday version: "It is better for a church to be small and serious than large and mixed." Tertullian, Novatian and the Donatists say yes; Augustine, Cyprian, Jerome and Optatus say no. (2) A second item would split people today far better: "If a pastor falls into serious sin, he should never lead a church again." Yes: Cyprian (Letter 67), Origen (Against Celsus 3.51: lapsed members never again given office), Martin of Tours (avoided the bishops), and Athanasius (pardon but not the clergy, in the second-chances file). No, as reported: Callistus, who would not depose a bishop even for a sin unto death (Hippolytus, Refutation 9.7). Augustine's anti-Donatist rule (a sinful minister's sacraments are still valid) is related but not the same question. (3) Best farthest-apart pairs for the reveal: Tertullian ("(the church) is a virgin!") against Augustine ("Let the good tolerate the bad"); Hippolytus against Callistus (the ark with dogs and wolves); Basil (the whole Church shares the guilt) against Moses the Black (the leaking basket of sand).

SOURCE FORMAT WARNINGS. New Advent inserts Bible references as link text inside passages (for example "Matthew 13:47-50"); every quote here was cut to avoid one. New Advent's ANF and NPNF texts are lightly modernised by its editor ("you" for "thou"). Archive.org OCR pages (Budge, Clarke, Burkitt) break lines and, in one Budge scan, double every space; the quotes match after collapsing whitespace. Budge prints a quotation mark at the start of every line of speech, so the Moses and Bessarion quotes contain stray marks; clean readings are in their context fields. The Moses and Antony quotes use the scan paradiseorgarden02ann (same as the second-chances file); Bessarion uses the cleaner scan ParadiseOfTheHolyFathersV2 of the same 1907 edition. The Tertullian original is copied from thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.pudicitia.shtml, which uses u for v. Originals were not found for the others (the Latin Library lacks Cyprian's letters, Jerome's dialogue and Augustine's sermons; augustinus.it refused the request); they are null rather than recalled from memory. The Tyconius Latin is cleaned from OCR, as its context says.

NOT USED, AND WHY. Origen, Homilies on Joshua 21.1 (the Church cannot be fully cleansed on earth): Latin via Rufinus and modern English only, not checked. Gregory the Great, Homilies on the Gospels (the good and the bad together in the Church): no public-domain English found and the Latin could not be fetched. Hilary on the tares (Commentary on Matthew 13): Latin only, not checked. Chrysostom, Homily 46 on Matthew: about not killing heretics, which belongs to another topic. Poemen (Budge 608) and the anonymous story of Timothy (Budge 359, who advised expelling a tempted brother and was then tempted himself): relevant in spirit, but about correction and an unnamed elder. Acesius the Novatianist at Nicaea (Socrates 1.10) is a genuine yes-voice, already in the second-chances file. No usable evidence found for Ignatius, Clement of Alexandria, Perpetua, Lactantius, Athanasius (beyond the second-chances letter), Ephrem, Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa, Macrina, Syncletica, Arsenius, Poemen, Evagrius, Paulinus, Boethius, Climacus or Isaac the Syrian.

HETERODOX AND DISPUTED. Tertullian (Montanist when writing On Modesty), Novatian and Sympronian (Novatianist schism), Petilian and Tyconius (Donatist schism, though Tyconius held the mixed view), and Pelagius (condemned 418 and 431). Origen's other teachings were condemned in 553. Hippolytus opposed Callistus as a rival bishop but is venerated as a martyr. The Callistus stance is an enemy's report. Book 7 of Optatus comes from a later edition and parts are doubted. The web-search budget was already used up when this task began, so everything here was reached by fetching known pages directly; no line depends on a search result.
